method: Thirty-four candidates survived a broad, prior-art-aware search. The pool is deliberately below the 100 ceiling: generic itinerary agents, video process mining, food-rescue matching, cooking assistants, board-game rule assistants, and ordinary visual food recognition were killed before this file. Every item has exactly one primary track and one primary sponsor prize.
score_legend: Positive dimensions are 0–10, higher is better. B and the final eight risk dimensions are 0–10, higher is worse. E/C/X/Q are sponsor eligibility, centrality, distinctive exploitation, and sponsor competitiveness; the qualitative sponsor_analysis and demo fields record depth, visibility, removal-test result, and sponsor-judge appeal. TF/TC are track fit and within-track competitiveness.

record_contract.identity: Contains the project name, one-sentence concept, and inline 15-second judge pitch after ‘pitch:’.
record_contract.pair: Explains why the declared single track and single primary sponsor are integral and why a commodity or alternate-sponsor substitution weakens the core interaction. It is not a second-prize target.
record_contract.ux: Contains first-ten-seconds, exact interaction, outcome, memorable moment, and practical use reason.
record_contract.demo: Contains live sequence, judge-visible proof, likely failure, and fallback.
record_contract.architecture: Names frontend, backend, models/APIs, data, algorithms, infrastructure, sponsor primitive, real-time behavior where relevant, and hardest technical component.
record_contract.sponsor_analysis: Applies the sponsor-removal test; E/C/X/Q/B preserve its numerical eligibility, centrality, distinctive-exploitation, sponsor-competitiveness, and bolt-on assessments.
record_contract.track_analysis: States track relevance, likely field alternative, and win condition.
record_contract.feasibility: Includes MVP, judge-ready, and polish hours plus setup, frontend, backend, model, integration, and demo risk.
record_contract.prior_art: Records closest known overlap and NOVEL / DIFFERENTIATED / CROWDED / ALREADY EXISTS classification; source evidence is centralized in research/prior_art/decision_evidence.md.
record_contract.competition: Records convergence, wrapper risk, strongest rival, and win condition.
record_contract.prob: Range estimates for MVP, polished demo conditional on MVP, live demo, chosen track, chosen sponsor, either target, overall, and no prize.

candidates.name: CycleClear
candidates.identity: Finds multi-person cycles that exchange scarce reservations, shifts, or equipment only when every leg settles; pitch: ‘Four people each get a better slot, or nobody loses theirs.’
candidates.user: Independent makerspaces, rehearsal rooms, and shared equipment communities.
candidates.problem: Bilateral swaps miss mutually beneficial 3–5-way cycles, and a participant can defect after others release a slot.
candidates.pair: Top-trading-cycle optimization is the product; a Solana program makes the cycle atomically settle on devnet. A central calendar or generic payment stack weakens the no-trusted-broker claim.
candidates.ux: First 10 seconds: a graph shows four incompatible swap requests. Users declare non-negotiables, see a highlighted cycle, approve it, and receive only their new reservation; the memorable moment is one all-or-nothing settlement moving all four nodes.
candidates.demo: Show the solver find a 4-way cycle, have four wallets approve, execute a visible devnet settlement, then show a declined consent leaving every reservation unchanged. Failure: wallet/cluster delay. Fallback: pre-funded devnet wallets and a live read of previously settled program state.
candidates.architecture: React graph UI; TypeScript cycle finder / top-trading-cycle variant; Anchor/Rust Solana program on devnet; Phantom or generated demo wallets; program state is the reservation ledger; websocket transaction confirmation. Hard part: multi-party atomic settlement and clear visualization.
candidates.sponsor_analysis: A real devnet program records each reservation right and settles every leg or none. Eligibility proof is an explorer signature, not an NFT or arbitrary hash.
candidates.track_analysis: The objective maximizes satisfiable preference cycles under resource constraints. Likely competitors are route schedulers; this wins if the graph and the atomicity are comprehensible.
candidates.feasibility: MVP 12h; judge-ready 17h; polish 6h. Risks: Anchor deployment and multiwallet UX; frontend medium, backend medium, model none, API low. Smallest version: one fixed 4-person cycle and two resource types.
candidates.prior_art: Closest: dynamic barter exchange and atomic-swap research; no close consumer micro-resource cycle-clearing product found. DIFFERENTIATED: reservation rights rather than crypto assets, with explicit all-party commitment.
candidates.competition: Independent convergence: unlikely outside algorithmic teams. AI-for-X: no. Stronger rival: a polished physical digital twin. It wins if the graph-to-ledger proof takes under 20 seconds.
candidates.kill: If Solana cannot settle an actual devnet cycle, this is a generic swap board.

candidates.name: ConstraintLens
candidates.identity: Turns a photographed, messy task board into typed constraints and exposes the smallest repair; pitch: ‘Point at the impossible plan and see the three changes that make it feasible.’
candidates.user: Student teams, event organizers, and workshop facilitators planning under hard time/resource constraints.
candidates.problem: A plan fails because constraints are implicit and contradictions remain invisible until late.
candidates.pair: Gemini vision and structured JSON extract constraints; an explicit SAT/ILP repair engine proves it is not a chat wrapper. Another model could technically replace Gemini, but the documented multimodal structured-output loop is the sponsor-visible core.
candidates.ux: A camera sees sticky notes and availability marks; within seconds the board becomes a constraint graph with one red unsatisfiable core. The user taps ‘smallest repair’ and sees a swap of two tasks.
candidates.demo: Photograph a controlled board, show Gemini JSON, run OR-Tools or a small SAT solver, move the three highlighted notes. Failure: vision latency. Fallback: locally cached Gemini structured result for the same photographed board, explicitly labeled as a replay.
candidates.architecture: React canvas; Gemini image input and JSON schema; Python/FastAPI solver with OR-Tools; task/people/time data; no unnecessary storage; hardest component is grounded extraction plus unsat-core explanation.
candidates.sponsor_analysis: Gemini must produce the constraint object from a real image; generic OCR alone cannot replace the semantic extraction.
candidates.track_analysis: Directly optimizes schedule feasibility. Competitors may offer pretty task boards; this wins if repair reasoning is visibly correct.
candidates.feasibility: MVP 8h; judge-ready 13h; polish 5h. Risks: extraction error and explanation clarity; frontend medium, backend low, model medium, API medium. Smallest version: a fixed board grammar.
candidates.prior_art: Whiteboard digitizers and schedulers exist, but camera-to-constraint-to-unsat-core is DIFFERENTIATED. Keep scope narrow.
candidates.competition: Independent convergence: moderate. AI-for-X: only if solver disappears. Stronger rival: a more useful field product. It wins on a crisp before/after.
candidates.kill: If the user must retype the board or the repair cannot be shown in ten seconds, kill it.

candidates.name: Resilience Canvas
candidates.identity: Injects a closure or no-show into a delivery plan and runs many failure worlds to choose the least brittle allocation; pitch: ‘Don’t optimize the sunny-day route—rehearse the failure.’
candidates.user: Small dispatch or volunteer logistics teams.
candidates.problem: Nominally optimal plans collapse when one road, driver, or pickup fails.
candidates.pair: A parallel Monte Carlo workload is the product and a visible Vultr compute job runs it; another hosting provider could run it, but a local/browser-only version would lose the scalable failure rehearsal.
candidates.ux: A manager drags a road closure onto a map; a cloud-job meter fills and five simulated futures collapse into one robust allocation. The ‘saved deliveries’ count is the memorable moment.
candidates.demo: Seed six deliveries and four drivers, inject a no-show, display naïve plan failure, run cloud scenarios, show resilient reallocation. Failure: GPU provisioning. Fallback: a Vultr CPU worker plus precomputed scenario traces.
candidates.architecture: React map; FastAPI job coordinator on Vultr; parallel Python simulations/OR-Tools; websocket job status; synthetic logistics data. Hard part: credible robust objective and a simple visual.
candidates.sponsor_analysis: Vultr run ID, worker fan-out, and live job metrics appear on stage. Static hosting alone does not qualify.
candidates.track_analysis: Robust allocation is plainly Optimization. Competitors may have easier apps; technical difficulty and demo make the case.
candidates.feasibility: MVP 16h; judge-ready 21h; polish 7h. Risks: cloud setup and overambitious simulation; frontend medium, backend high, model none, API medium. Smallest version: one closure and 100 CPU scenarios.
candidates.prior_art: Robust-routing research is close, but a small live failure-rehearsal interface is DIFFERENTIATED.
candidates.competition: Independent convergence: low. AI-for-X: no. Stronger rival: a validated physical simulation. It wins only if computation visibly changes the recommendation.
candidates.kill: If the cloud job is ornamental or it becomes a static route planner, kill it.

candidates.name: ConsentSolver
candidates.identity: Finds the best group plan without exposing raw calendars, budgets, or preferences; pitch: ‘Grant availability, not your life story, and see the feasible region grow.’
candidates.user: Friends and small teams coordinating a plan with private constraints.
candidates.problem: Scheduling tools force people to overshare to get a feasible result.
candidates.pair: Protected calendar/resource APIs expose only scoped fields through Auth0 delegated authorization. A generic scheduler loses the key permission-bound optimization interaction.
candidates.ux: Four people toggle ‘free/busy only’ grants; the feasible plan surface grows or shrinks without revealing any event title. A denied agent action visibly leaves a blank, not a leak.
candidates.demo: Connect one real calendar or protected mock resource, grant scopes, solve a meeting, revoke one grant, recompute. Failure: external OAuth. Fallback: a first-party protected API with real Auth0 claims.
candidates.architecture: Next.js; Auth0 Universal Login/RBAC or Token Vault; FastAPI constraint solver; mock calendar API with field-level scopes; audit trace. Hard part: real protected-resource boundary.
candidates.sponsor_analysis: Auth0 must protect actual data and control the solver/agent’s query permissions. Login alone fails.
candidates.track_analysis: Optimizes feasibility under consent constraints; likely judges will understand after one revoke/recompute.
candidates.feasibility: MVP 12h; judge-ready 17h; polish 5h. Risks: Auth0 tenant configuration; frontend medium, backend medium, model none, API medium. Smallest version: two people and availability-only.
candidates.prior_art: Doodle/When2Meet are crowded, but permission-bounded feasible-region feedback is DIFFERENTIATED.
candidates.competition: Independent convergence: low. AI-for-X: no. Stronger rival: Travel Proxy’s cleaner narrative. It wins if privacy is immediately visual.
candidates.kill: If Auth0 is only login or no protected resource changes the answer, kill it.

candidates.name: UndoPoint
candidates.identity: Explains the first event that made a live plan infeasible and the minimum reversals; pitch: ‘Your schedule broke here—and here is the smallest undo.’
candidates.user: Dispatchers and teams operating an allocation plan that changes throughout a day.
candidates.problem: A planner can recompute a solution but cannot explain which update created an impossible state.
candidates.pair: Atlas change streams and durable event documents make causal replay visible; a static relational snapshot cannot naturally expose the evolving event trail.
candidates.ux: A live event stream turns red at one update; a scrubber jumps to the causal change and highlights two reversal options.
candidates.demo: Seed a small shift/resource plan, add successive changes through two clients, have the system locate the first infeasible event and show minimal reversals. Failure: stream configuration. Fallback: Atlas reads of an event log with polling labeled as fallback.
candidates.architecture: React timeline; Atlas event collection/change streams; Python incremental feasibility checker; websocket updates; min-hitting-set style reversal search. Hard part: explaining causality rather than merely rerunning.
candidates.sponsor_analysis: Committed Atlas changes trigger the proof; plain users/settings storage would not.
candidates.track_analysis: A direct optimization debugging product. It beats dashboards only if ‘why now?’ is answerable instantly.
candidates.feasibility: MVP 12h; judge-ready 17h; polish 5h. Risks: causal algorithm explanation; frontend medium, backend medium, API low. Smallest version: one capacity constraint.
candidates.prior_art: Event-sourced planning exists, but causal infeasibility debugging has no close product found. NOVEL with search limits.
candidates.competition: Independent convergence: low. AI-for-X: no. Stronger rival: CycleClear’s live chain. It wins if data mutation visibly causes failure.
candidates.kill: If users ask why they would not just rerun the optimizer, kill it.

candidates.name: LineCheck
candidates.identity: A solver asks the one stakeholder question that resolves a plan fastest through a live voice exchange; pitch: ‘Don’t call everyone—call the person whose answer unlocks the plan.’
candidates.user: Small volunteer coordinators and event planners.
candidates.problem: Planners waste time gathering low-value information while a single missing answer blocks the plan.
candidates.pair: The voice interaction is the action loop, not narration: the system selects and conducts the information-gathering call. Text forms weaken the time-critical feature.
candidates.ux: A blocked plan points to one person; the person answers a short voice prompt and the allocation snaps into a solution.
candidates.demo: Show three unknowns, rank information gain, role-play an ElevenLabs exchange for one answer, recompute. Failure: STT/TTS latency. Fallback: prerecorded but genuinely generated two-way audio with a visible transcript.
candidates.architecture: React plan canvas; uncertainty/information-gain heuristic; ElevenLabs speech engine; FastAPI solver; light event store. Hard part: making the chosen question visibly valuable.
candidates.sponsor_analysis: ElevenLabs manages the bidirectional voice exchange and interruption, shown as the central action.
candidates.track_analysis: Optimization of information acquisition is real but abstract; track fit depends on explaining the objective quickly.
candidates.feasibility: MVP 12h; judge-ready 16h; polish 5h. Risks: voice reliability and abstract pitch; frontend medium, backend medium, model low. Smallest version: three stakeholders, binary answers.
candidates.prior_art: Voice dispatch exists; solver-directed question selection appears NOVEL.
candidates.competition: Independent convergence: low. AI-for-X: no. Stronger rival: a more tangible physical problem. It wins if the before/after schedule is vivid.
candidates.kill: If a text form can replace the voice interaction without losing urgency, kill it.

candidates.name: Entitlement Auction
candidates.identity: Allocates scarce bundles—such as a room plus equipment—in sealed preferences and atomically settles the whole bundle; pitch: ‘No one gives up their half until the entire bundle is real.’
candidates.user: Independent shared-resource communities with coupled reservations.
candidates.problem: A desired resource bundle fails when partial booking creates stranded pieces and participants distrust a coordinator.
candidates.pair: The solver chooses a welfare-maximizing bundle allocation and Solana program enforces sealed bids/atomic settlement. A normal booking table has weaker cross-party trust proof.
candidates.ux: Users enter private valuations, a bundle board flips to a conflict-free allocation, and the program settles one matched bundle only after approvals.
candidates.demo: Run a fixed combinatorial allocation, show sealed values, settle on devnet, demonstrate a missing signer cancels the bundle. Failure: program complexity. Fallback: constrain to two bundles and three bidders.
candidates.architecture: React auction UI; winner-determination brute force/ILP; Anchor program with commitments/reveal; devnet wallets. Hard part: sealed-bid UX and safe, understandable program state.
candidates.sponsor_analysis: A devnet commitment/reveal and all-or-nothing program state are necessary—not payments.
candidates.track_analysis: Combinatorial allocation is exact Optimization, though the explanation burden is higher than CycleClear.
candidates.feasibility: MVP 14h; judge-ready 19h; polish 6h. Risks: cryptographic reveal / scope; frontend medium, backend medium. Smallest version: three users, two bundles.
candidates.prior_art: Combinatorial auctions and booking platforms exist; program-enforced microbundle settlement is DIFFERENTIATED.
candidates.competition: Independent convergence: low. AI-for-X: no. Stronger rival: CycleClear with simpler graph story.
candidates.kill: If values, wallet approval, or settlement are mocked, kill it.

candidates.name: Proxy Passport
candidates.identity: A traveler grants an agent or trusted helper narrow, expiring authority during a disruption; pitch: ‘Let it find a seat, never let it spend or cancel without you.’
candidates.user: Travelers who need help rebooking while stressed or offline.
candidates.problem: Sharing credentials gives a helper/agent too much power, but refusing delegation makes disruptions harder to resolve.
candidates.pair: Travel is the human stakes; Auth0 Token Vault/delegated OAuth and approval make the core boundary. A generic assistant or login cannot replace the permission contract.
candidates.ux: First 10 seconds: a traveler drags ‘search’, ‘hold’, and ‘cancel’ onto a passport card. The agent finds a new route, a hold is allowed, and a cancellation triggers explicit approval.
candidates.demo: Use a mock airline API plus actual Auth0 protected scopes; show connected-account/Token-Vault flow if ready, allow a hold, deny a cancellation, approve it, and show an audit. Failure: provider OAuth. Fallback: a first-party mock provider with real Auth0 authorization.
candidates.architecture: Next.js travel disruption board; Auth0 Universal Login, delegated tokens/Token Vault or RBAC fallback, CIBA/approval if accessible; FastAPI mock airline tool; audit log. Hard part: prove the agent never sees credentials.
candidates.sponsor_analysis: Auth0 controls every agent tool call and approval, visibly. This is stronger than a travel app with social login.
candidates.track_analysis: The permissions answer a real travel-disruption moment. Likely competitors are itinerary generators; it wins through trust and action, not recommendations.
candidates.feasibility: MVP 12h; judge-ready 17h; polish 6h. Risks: Token Vault/CIBA setup and demo external provider; frontend medium, backend medium, model optional. Smallest version: one traveler, allowed search, denied cancel.
candidates.prior_art: Travel agency role controls and general agent authorization exist; consumer per-trip action-bounded delegation is DIFFERENTIATED, not unprecedented.
candidates.competition: Independent convergence: low. AI-for-X: only if it turns into chat. Stronger rival: a more tangible travel visual. It wins if the denied action makes judges gasp.
candidates.kill: If it lacks actual delegated authorization/approval and only shows roles, kill it.

candidates.name: Delayscape
candidates.identity: Chooses a trip for survival probability under missed connections rather than nominal ETA; pitch: ‘The fastest route is not the route that gets you there.’
candidates.user: Travelers with tight multimodal connections.
candidates.problem: Route planners optimize expected arrival while hiding how fragile transfers are.
candidates.pair: A parallel cloud simulation evaluates thousands of failure worlds; a normal route planner would not expose the resilience computation.
candidates.ux: Two routes have equal ETAs; a resilience meter shows one has 82% arrival probability after sampled delays. A closure changes the heat map in real time.
candidates.demo: Seed a rail/flight network, run scenarios on Vultr, compare nominal and robust route. Failure: compute. Fallback: a small CPU job with stored scenario frames.
candidates.architecture: React network map; Vultr workers; stochastic graph simulation; route data fixture; websocket job events. Hard part: legible probability rather than fake precision.
candidates.sponsor_analysis: The cloud fan-out must be visible in job state and outputs.
candidates.track_analysis: Direct Traveling benefit. It loses if judges see a standard itinerary planner.
candidates.feasibility: MVP 16h; judge-ready 21h; polish 6h. Risks: scope/data, cloud setup; frontend medium, backend high. Smallest version: six-node rail graph.
candidates.prior_art: Robust transit work and standby tools are close; a generalized resilience visualizer is DIFFERENTIATED.
candidates.competition: Independent convergence: moderate. AI-for-X: no. Stronger rival: a mature route app.
candidates.kill: If it becomes a normal route planner, kill it.

candidates.name: Arrival Witness
candidates.identity: Compares itinerary context with a live camera view of a confusing gate, entrance, or transfer point; pitch: ‘Your ticket says platform 7—your camera proves where platform 7 actually is.’
candidates.user: Travelers navigating rapidly changing transport spaces.
candidates.problem: Text itineraries and physical wayfinding cues diverge, leaving travelers to infer whether the plan still matches reality.
candidates.pair: Gemini must compare visual scene evidence to itinerary context and output a structured mismatch/next-action object. A static camera chatbot is insufficient.
candidates.ux: A ticket and station image arrive together; the UI draws a red mismatch line from ‘Gate B’ to the live ‘Gate C’ sign and gives one evidence-backed next step.
candidates.demo: Use a known image/ticket fixture and Gemini structured output; show a true match then a mismatch. Failure: vision latency. Fallback: cached answer paired with displayed original request.
candidates.architecture: Mobile React UI; Gemini vision plus JSON schema; small itinerary parser; confidence/evidence UI. Hard part: grounded, conservative answers.
candidates.sponsor_analysis: Multimodal comparison—not text generation—is demonstrably central.
candidates.track_analysis: Clear Traveling story, but Google Lens/Live View are close.
candidates.feasibility: MVP 8h; judge-ready 12h; polish 5h. Risks: prior-art and hallucination; frontend medium, backend low, model medium. Smallest version: two predetermined stations.
candidates.prior_art: Google Lens/Live View are close. It survives as DIFFERENTIATED only on itinerary-to-scene consistency checking.
candidates.competition: Independent convergence: high. AI-for-X: danger. Stronger rival: Google’s own product.
candidates.kill: If a one-photo response is the whole experience, kill it.

candidates.name: StaleMap
candidates.identity: Represents travel facts as time-decaying claims so an old elevator or entrance report never poses as current truth; pitch: ‘Accessibility is not a pin—it is evidence with an expiration date.’
candidates.user: Travelers who rely on elevators, step-free entrances, or sensory conditions.
candidates.problem: Static accessibility maps hide that a facility may be temporarily unusable and conflict reports often outlive their evidence.
candidates.pair: Atlas geo queries, event documents, TTL/expiry, and change streams make the changing evidence graph and live route update load-bearing. A generic map backend weakens the visible data system.
candidates.ux: First 10 seconds: a step-free route is green. A teammate reports an elevator outage; its confidence/red freshness mark appears and the route re-runs across the map. A later photo expires or restores confidence.
candidates.demo: Two clients submit conflicting reports in a seed mini-map; Atlas change stream updates confidence and A* route choice. Failure: stream/network. Fallback: seeded Atlas read with an honest refresh button.
candidates.architecture: React MapLibre map; Atlas 2dsphere event collection, TTL and change streams; FastAPI confidence model/A*; mock OSM graph. Hard part: evidence decay and conflict explanation.
candidates.sponsor_analysis: Geo, live change events, and expiry are all observable, not a users collection.
candidates.track_analysis: Traveling is central and meaningful. Likely competitors are accessibility directories; it wins if route alteration is immediate.
candidates.feasibility: MVP 12h; judge-ready 17h; polish 6h. Risks: map integration, confidence design; frontend medium, backend medium, API medium. Smallest version: four nodes, two incidents.
candidates.prior_art: Accessibility maps and transit alerts exist. DIFFERENTIATED by expiring, conflicting firsthand evidence that changes a route.
candidates.competition: Independent convergence: moderate. AI-for-X: no. Stronger rival: polished existing accessibility apps. It wins if ‘truth expires’ sticks.
candidates.kill: If a new report does not visibly change confidence and routing, kill it.

candidates.name: LostLoop
candidates.identity: Matches lost-item witness reports by time, location, and visual/text similarity, then explains why the match is plausible; pitch: ‘Turn three uncertain sightings into one defensible lead.’
candidates.user: Travel hubs and their passengers managing lost property.
candidates.problem: Lost-and-found reports are fragmented across locations and descriptions, causing missed matches or unsafe false positives.
candidates.pair: Atlas geo-temporal queries and vector/text retrieval assemble witnesses as evidence; generic storage loses the cross-witness retrieval feature.
candidates.ux: A lost red backpack report receives two witness signals; a map/time ribbon shows why one is likely and one is stale. The user sees the minimal safe next verification step.
candidates.demo: Seed three reports and add a phone photo/location; show Atlas candidate retrieval and scoring. Failure: vector-index setup. Fallback: text+geo match without vector search.
candidates.architecture: React map/timeline; Atlas 2dsphere and search/vector index; FastAPI ranking; photo descriptors; consent/redaction controls. Hard part: false-positive and privacy handling.
candidates.sponsor_analysis: Atlas indexes are the matching engine, visible through candidate provenance.
candidates.track_analysis: A direct travel-hub problem; demo must avoid claiming recovery certainty.
candidates.feasibility: MVP 12h; judge-ready 17h; polish 5h. Risks: privacy and vector indexing; frontend medium, backend medium. Smallest version: exact colors and locations.
candidates.prior_art: Airport lost-and-found systems and Tile exist; cross-witness geo-temporal retrieval is DIFFERENTIATED.
candidates.competition: Independent convergence: low. AI-for-X: no. Stronger rival: StaleMap has clearer impact.
candidates.kill: If false positives and privacy are hand-waved, kill it.

candidates.name: RepairRelay
candidates.identity: A traveler, local, and remote helper use a three-role voice relay that manages turns and asks only confidence-verified questions; pitch: ‘Translation is easy; repairing a misunderstanding is the journey.’
candidates.user: Travelers in a disruption who need a local and remote supporter to coordinate.
candidates.problem: Ordinary translation does not manage ambiguous multi-party repairs, interruptions, and confidence.
candidates.pair: Realtime voice presence and controlled turn-taking are the interaction. A text translation app cannot provide the hands-busy, multi-party loop.
candidates.ux: Three voices occupy a shared live transcript; the relay interrupts only to ask the one clarifying question needed before relaying a decision.
candidates.demo: Role-play a missed-connection misunderstanding in two languages, show turn assignment and corrected confirmation. Failure: live speech quality. Fallback: prepared multilingual audio with a live turn UI.
candidates.architecture: WebRTC/ElevenLabs speech engine; turn state machine; transcript/confidence controls; lightweight scenario API. Hard part: not turning it into ordinary translation.
candidates.sponsor_analysis: ElevenLabs handles speech recognition/synthesis and makes the voices operational state.
candidates.track_analysis: Natural but competitive Travel use. Judges must see repair rather than novelty audio.
candidates.feasibility: MVP 12h; judge-ready 17h; polish 6h. Risks: multilingual latency and demo timing; frontend medium, backend medium. Smallest version: English plus one language, three roles.
candidates.prior_art: Pocketalk/Google Interpreter are close; contextual three-party repair is DIFFERENTIATED but risky.
candidates.competition: Independent convergence: moderate. AI-for-X: no. Stronger rival: a real translation product.
candidates.kill: If it resembles ordinary live translation, kill it.

candidates.name: DetourPact
candidates.identity: Lets a group commit contingency funds under a quorum, price cap, and alternate-route condition; pitch: ‘Agree on the backup before the missed train makes everyone panic.’
candidates.user: Groups traveling together with shared disruption costs.
candidates.problem: Groups cannot pre-commit fair contingencies without one person carrying the financial and social risk.
candidates.pair: A Solana program holds a conditional group commitment and releases only after the stated route/price condition. Ordinary expense splitting misses the trust primitive.
candidates.ux: Friends set a $120 cap and a 3-of-4 quorum; a simulated cancellation hits, the contract exposes the approved alternative, and the group sees who approved.
candidates.demo: Create pact on devnet, show cancellation oracle fixture, obtain quorum signatures, settle/expire. Failure: condition oracle. Fallback: a signed mock disruption event clearly labeled.
candidates.architecture: React pact UI; Anchor conditional program; devnet wallets; route fixture/attested event; threshold state. Hard part: no fake oracle or financial claims.
candidates.sponsor_analysis: Program state and transaction evidence are core; no tokens/speculation.
candidates.track_analysis: Travel disruption makes the commitment concrete, although general escrow products are close.
candidates.feasibility: MVP 13h; judge-ready 18h; polish 6h. Risks: smart contract and scope; frontend medium, backend medium. Smallest version: fixed price condition plus 2-of-3 quorum.
candidates.prior_art: Shared-expense and conditional escrow products exist; group disruption commitment is DIFFERENTIATED.
candidates.competition: Independent convergence: low. AI-for-X: no. Stronger rival: CycleClear’s less financially sensitive story.
candidates.kill: If the condition is manually asserted and the chain adds no trust property, kill it.

candidates.name: Triangulate
candidates.identity: Separate witnesses submit image, audio, and text evidence; Gemini builds a claim graph, flags contradiction, and requests the next most informative observation; pitch: ‘Don’t vote on rumors—collect the one fact that resolves them.’
candidates.user: Teams coordinating around an uncertain live observation.
candidates.problem: Groups treat unverified reports as shared truth or waste attention collecting redundant evidence.
candidates.pair: Gemini transforms multimodal evidence into strict claims/confidence and selects a discriminating next observation. A chat summary lacks the active-verification loop.
candidates.ux: Three phones disagree about a red claim; the graph points one teammate at a photo task. That photo changes the claim from red to green for everyone.
candidates.demo: Submit staged audio/text/photo reports, show structured claim graph, add requested photo, show confidence update. Failure: multimodal API. Fallback: cached Gemini JSON with original evidence visible.
candidates.architecture: React multiplayer board; Gemini multimodal + JSON schema; information-gain heuristic; websocket room; evidence files. Hard part: evidence provenance and conservative wording.
candidates.sponsor_analysis: Gemini's multimodal structured output is central and visible.
candidates.track_analysis: The group is the sensor network; it cannot work as a single-user assistant.
candidates.feasibility: MVP 12h; judge-ready 17h; polish 6h. Risks: Gemini latency, claim grounding; frontend medium, backend medium. Smallest version: three claims and one requested observation.
candidates.prior_art: Ushahidi/crisis maps collect reports; active multimodal disambiguation is DIFFERENTIATED.
candidates.competition: Independent convergence: low–medium. AI-for-X: only if it merely summarizes. Stronger rival: a more physical multiplayer demo.
candidates.kill: If it summarizes reports instead of assigning a next verification task, kill it.

candidates.name: RumorClock
candidates.identity: Shows what a group knows, what is merely claimed, and what has gone stale as evidence streams in; pitch: ‘A shared room where certainty decays unless someone refreshes it.’
candidates.user: Teams managing changing, imperfectly observed facts.
candidates.problem: Shared docs preserve statements but not evidence freshness or epistemic status.
candidates.pair: Atlas event documents/change streams power a live epistemic state; time decay and provenance require mutable shared data, not a chat history.
candidates.ux: A live claim card visibly fades from verified to stale until a teammate adds evidence; all rooms update together.
candidates.demo: Three clients add/verify/contradict a claim; change stream updates the wall and a timer decay changes state. Failure: live stream. Fallback: timed Atlas fetches.
candidates.architecture: React room; Atlas collections/change streams and TTL; FastAPI confidence rules; websocket broadcaster. Hard part: making an abstract truth model emotionally legible.

candidates.name: Babel Relay

candidates.name: Consent Relay

candidates.competition: Independent convergence: low. AI-for-X: no. Stronger rival: Proxy Passport's concrete travel stakes.
candidates.kill: If it feels like an IAM admin console, kill it.

candidates.name: ManySight

candidates.name: Ask Once
candidates.identity: Turns a photo or handwritten donation label into an evidence-tagged ingredient graph, then asks the staffer the single question that unlocks the most safely matchable portions; pitch: ‘Do not guess what food is safe—ask the one question that changes the answer.’
candidates.user: Food-rescue and community-kitchen staff receiving ambiguously labeled donated food.
candidates.problem: Staff discard or underuse donations because they cannot safely infer uncertain ingredients or decide which clarification is worth interrupting a donor for.
candidates.pair: Gemini vision produces a structured evidence/uncertainty graph from the label; a constrained matching/information-gain engine chooses the question. Generic food rescue matching is deliberately excluded—the question-selection loop is the product.
candidates.ux: A photo of an ambiguous tray label produces red uncertainty nodes and only one of four household matches. The app asks ‘Does the sauce contain sesame?’; a human answer turns the graph green and enables four matches.
candidates.demo: Scan a controlled handwritten label, display Gemini structured evidence, show conservative allocation, enter one human-confirmed answer, recompute matchable portions. Failure: handwriting vision. Fallback: a photo with prewarmed Gemini response and visible raw evidence; never fabricate a safety answer.

Hard part: uncertainty calibration and human-confirmed gating.

candidates.track_analysis: The problem and outcome are unambiguously Food. Likely competitors are food-rescue apps; it beats them only if the change from one answer is shown.
candidates.feasibility: MVP 10h; judge-ready 15h; polish 6h. Risks: unsafe framing, Gemini output consistency, label fixture. Frontend medium, backend medium, model medium, integration medium. Smallest version: one tray, two uncertain ingredients, four household constraints.
candidates.prior_art: Food-rescue platforms and AI photo matchers exist, including RescueRoute/Dashwill/Replate. DIFFERENTIATED only by conservative evidence graph plus maximum-information question selection, with no automatic safety guess.
candidates.competition: Independent convergence: low for the exact mechanism. AI-for-X: no if the graph/optimizer is on screen. Stronger rival: a mature food-rescue platform; ours wins only with the single-question transformation.
candidates.kill: If the team presents inferred allergens as fact, or if a generic matching dashboard is the demo, kill it.
